logline: A small-time Japanese con artist gets outplayed by a superior French swindler and is recruited into an international ring that targets corrupt tycoons and crime bosses across Los Angeles, Singapore, London, and Tokyo.

renewal.note: The original 23-episode series concluded in September 2020. A four-episode sequel ONA, Great Pretender: Razbliuto, was released in February-March 2024, completing the story.

bollymeter.basis: A 100 percent Rotten Tomatoes score from 7 critics and a 92 percent audience score reflect genuine enthusiasm for the heist structure and globe-trotting style; IMDb lands at 7.8, capturing a modest audience-critic gap. Anime News Network graded it A-, calling it fun, bingeable con artist hijinks.

pull_quotes.text: Fun, bingeable con artist hijinks that will keep you guessing, in a setting that feels almost real.
Great Pretender understands that knowing when to make an exit is just as important as nailing the first impression.

seasons.review_body: Great Pretender dropped on Netflix globally in August 2020. The original run of 23 episodes is structured in four self-contained con arcs, moving through Los Angeles, Singapore, London, and Tokyo. The series balances candy-bright visuals from WIT Studio against a narrative full of moral murkiness, while its suspense builds deliberately through each scheme. For heist-genre fans, the episodic arc structure rewards binge watching, with late reveals that can feel meticulously arranged. Viewers often revisit the show for its con-artist hijinks and the momentum of its self-contained setups.

episode_reviews.title: Case 1_1: Los Angeles Connection
episode_reviews.review_body: Great Pretender's premiere aired June 2, 2020 on Fuji TV and Netflix, produced by WIT Studio. The episode dropped Makoto Edamura into an attempted Los Angeles street con that immediately backfired, establishing the show's central inversion of the heist genre from its first scene: the protagonist is the mark rather than the master, and the confidence of his initial position in the episode was engineered to collapse in a way that reorganised the audience's understanding of every prior character introduction. The WIT Studio visual direction - candy-bright Los Angeles rendered in a palette that was almost aggressively stylised against the moral murkiness of the show's narrative - was announced in the premiere's first sequence and maintained consistently through the series. CBR identified the show's 'irreverence for society and law that makes crime just seem so much fun.' The LA arc's structure as a self-contained con case introduced the show's episodic format and established that Great Pretender would reward binge watching by hiding its reveals inside individual cases before deploying them across the full series.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere drops Makoto Edamura into an attempted street con that immediately backfires, establishing the show's playful inversion of the genre - the protagonist is the mark, not the master. The visual direction signals WIT Studio's ambition from the first frame.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The moment Makoto realises he has been outplayed by Laurent - the entire premise snaps into place.

critic_note.text: It has an irreverence for society and law that makes crime just seem so much fun.

episode_reviews.title: Case 4_1: Wizard of Far East
episode_reviews.review_body: Great Pretender's fourth and final arc premiered November 25, 2020 on Netflix globally and turned the show's con-artist formula against itself: the team's backstory - the origin of how Laurent, Abbie, Cynthia and Makoto came to work together - became the subject of the Tokyo arc rather than the context for a new external target. WIT Studio structured the arc as a series of retroactive reveals that recontextualised decisions made in the three preceding cases, a formal choice consistent with the con-artist genre's fondness for the show-within-a-show. The emotional payoff the series had been building toward arrived here through character revelation rather than plot mechanics - the question the show had deferred across fourteen episodes, about what Laurent was actually trying to accomplish and why Makoto's presence in the team was necessary to it, received an answer that made the con that ran across the entire 23-episode series visible only from the final arc's vantage point.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The fourth and final case turns the show's con-artist formula against itself, bringing the team's backstory into the foreground. This arc provides the emotional payoff the series had been building toward.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The reveal that recontextualises the team's origin - the con the audience did not see coming.
